GHSA-R2XF-8XR9-62GW.8c4a687083babd105464d2d55b34f2cd1f22e6d3:
GROOVY-12349: groovysh: guard /grep's regex matching against backtracking

Ported from JLine 1d5fc309, which our fork of PosixCommands predates. The
upstream commit cites GHSA-r2xf-8xr9-62gw, GHSA-2v9w-34q6-wpqx,
GHSA-ph9c-7hw9-vhhw and GHSA-5q95-hrpc-m3w3, and the fork carried the
shape those describe.

grep built its pattern as ".*" + pattern + ".*" and matched that against
the whole line. Both halves of that are wrong: the intent is to find the
pattern in the line, which find() says directly, and the wrapping gives a
backtracking engine more to explore for no gain. The wrapping goes, -x
keeps the anchored form and matches(), and everything else finds.

Both matchers now run through SafeRegex, which wraps the input in a
CharSequence that checks a deadline as the engine reads it, so a pattern
that would otherwise run away gives up after 1.5s. The highlighting
matcher catches the timeout and emits the rest of the line unhighlighted,
as upstream does, rather than losing the line. SafeRegex comes from
jline-terminal, which groovysh already depends on directly, so this takes
upstream's implementation rather than adding our own.

Tests pin the two matching paths that separate here, find() and the
anchored matches(), and invert alongside them. They read output with the
SGR sequences stripped rather than with colouring off, so the highlighting
path, which is the one holding the new try/catch, stays covered.

Not demonstrated: a pattern that actually trips the deadline. Several
classic catastrophic patterns, including (a+)+b and (a|aa)+$, complete
immediately on JDK 17 whether wrapped or not, so the guard is defensive
here rather than shown to fire.

CVE-2020-17521.e03c74e720146da74ea573a3fc35649d726fe9f0:
GROOVY-12335: groovysh: keep session state readable only by its owner

The shell's history records every line typed at the prompt, and /save
writes the session's bound variables to groovysh.ser. Both were created at
whatever the ambient umask allowed - measured on a default umask of 022,
~/.groovy came out 0755 and groovysh_history 0644 - so on a shared host
any local user could read what had been typed and what it evaluated to.
That is the class of exposure behind CVE-2020-17521, and the §7 local
adversary this project already recognises.

The state directory is now created 0700 and both files 0600. The history
file is created before JLine opens it, so the history lands in a file that
was owner-only from the start rather than being tightened afterwards.

A file that already exists is tightened only when it is currently more
permissive than owner-only, so a mode the user chose deliberately - a
stricter one, say - is left as it is. Permission changes are best effort:
a state file that cannot be adjusted is still a usable state file, and the
shell should not refuse to start over one.

Only files this project creates are covered. JLine writes aliases.json and
pipeline-names.json into the same directory and still creates them 0644;
they are reachable only through the state directory, so a fresh install
gets the 0700 directory as its defence, but an installation whose
~/.groovy already exists keeps the directory mode it has. Tightening a
directory that also holds the Grape caches is not a decision to take
silently, so it is left alone here.
